sources.entry: The HTTP crash course nobody asked for

summary.title: The HTTP crash course nobody asked for
summary.one_liner: Learn how HTTP/1.1 works at the TCP level, why writing a proxy is hard, and how to make raw HTTP and HTTPS requests from Rust with reqwest, hyper, rustls and plain sockets.
takeaways: HTTP/1.1 is plain text over a TCP socket: a request line, headers terminated by CRLF, then an optional body sized by Content-Length or chunked encoding.

Writing an HTTP proxy means making many opinionated choices about header validation, body buffering, compression and transfer encoding, and guarding against resource exhaustion attacks like Slowloris.
You can send raw HTTP with nc and HTTPS with openssl s_client, and inspect traffic with tcpdump and Wireshark.
The article builds up from high-level reqwest to hyper to hand-rolled HTTP/1.1 over rustls, showing what each layer does.
summary.summary:
The author, who maintains an HTTP/S/2 proxy at work, explains HTTP/1.1 from the ground up: TCP connections, request and response headers, Host, Connection, content length, HEAD/GET/POST methods, and chunked encoding. He then discusses the many design decisions and attack surfaces involved in proxying HTTP/1.1 for a CDN. The hands-on part sends raw requests with nc and openssl s_client, and then builds up Rust clients from reqwest to hyper to a manual implementation over rustls, verifying the traffic with tcpdump and Wireshark. The page was last updated about four years ago and is cut off before the manual implementation is finished.</summary>
